title: Sunk Costs: why you must ignore past spend and kill what isn't working
summary: Jason Cohen explains that sunk costs (money, time and effort already spent and unrecoverable) should be ignored when deciding what to do next, yet human loss aversion makes us cling to them. He applies it to startup situations: pet features, marketing slogans, bad hires, endless A/B iteration, and long-shot enterprise deals.

principles.text: Ignore sunk costs: spent money and effort is gone whatever you do next, so decide only on future costs and benefits.
principles.quote: "Sunk Cost" is money you've already spent and cannot get back.

principles.text: Sunk-cost bias is human nature, not just big-company politics. Startups fall for it too, so be vigilant.
principles.quote: It's not just politics, it's human nature.

principles.text: Kill a feature customers don't care about, even if it was hard to build and you're proud of it.
principles.quote: But that effort is sunk whether or not it's the right fit for your product; kill the feature.

principles.text: Don't force a clever idea, like a slogan, into the business just to avoid wasting it. Learn to throw things out.
principles.quote: You don't want to "waste" this great concept; surely you can use it somehow, somewhere? No. As with all writing, you have to learn how to throw things out.

principles.text: Don't keep a bad hire because of the effort spent finding and training them. Prolonging it is worse, for you and for them.
principles.quote: You can't get that time back, and yes this is one of the most expensive mistakes you can make, but even worse is prolonging the inevitable.

principles.text: Drop a long-running big-name sale that keeps finding reasons not to buy. It signals poor fit; you need profitable customers and advocates.
principles.quote: All this is just an indicator that you don't have a good fit; this time-suck isn't going to vanish once they buy. Let it go.
